sentences: Under the light of the moon, a great cape rises out of the sea and emerges from the darkness.
This is the sea at the far northern edge of Europe.
The painting is The North Cape by Moonlight, by the Norwegian painter Peder Balke.
It was painted in oil on canvas in 1848, and it measures 62 centimetres high and 85 centimetres wide.
It belongs to The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, where it hangs among the European paintings in gallery 807.
Look first at the cape itself.
We are not standing on land; we are looking up at the cliffs from the water.
That is exactly how Balke saw it with his own eyes.
In the nineteenth century, people believed the North Cape was the northernmost point of Europe, the very end of the continent.
Now look at the light and the dark.
The places the moonlight touches and the places it cannot reach are divided into broad areas, which makes the picture both simple and intense.
This dark palette and free, expressive brushwork are characteristic of Balke's mature style.
His mentor was Johan Christian Dahl, the leading master of Norwegian landscape painting.
Where Dahl recorded nature in a calm and restrained way, Balke painted the same northern nature far more dramatically, sometimes almost like a vision.
Balke travelled to the North Cape by ship only once, in 1832.
The overwhelming impression of that journey became the touchstone of his art for the rest of his life.
This painting was made sixteen years afterwards, from memory and imagination.
When this painting, or another version of it, was shown in Oslo in the autumn of 1848, a critic praised it both for the subject itself and for the singular way the artist had chosen his moment.
Balke was born into a poor family in Norway in 1804 and died in 1887.

In the 1840s, in Paris, he received a major commission from the French king Louis-Philippe for scenes of northern Norway, but when the revolution of 1848 drove the king from his throne, the commission was abandoned.
After that his career as a painter faltered, and he turned to building affordable housing for working people and to politics.
His art was largely forgotten for more than a century, until exhibitions in London and New York brought it back to light.
This canvas was given to the Met in 2019, in celebration of the museum's 150th anniversary.
Step back and look again.
This is the moonlit night of a painter who saw this sea only once and painted it for the rest of his life.
Think of a landscape you saw just once, long ago, that is still vivid in your mind today.
